This supplement lists the **symbols** of the book and the rules for writing them. Each
concept has one symbol in every chapter, practical, case study, supplement and slide, so
that an equation reads the same wherever you meet it. The tables give the symbol, what it
means and the chapter where it first appears; the chapter explains the concept, and the
[Glossary](glossary.qmd) defines the terms in words.

Some common letters ($a$, $b$, $c$, $k$, $x$, $p$) are short and convenient, so an
exercise or an example may give one of them a slightly different meaning for a specific
problem. When that happens, the text of the exercise or example says what the letter means
there. Those local meanings are not listed here.

# Data and random variables

A capital letter is a random variable, a quantity whose value is uncertain before we
observe it. The same letter in lower case is a possible or observed value of it. A sample
without predictors is written with $X$; when a model has a predictor or groups, the
response is $Y$ and the predictor is $x$. A model may use a capital that reminds us of the
quantity (for example the initial of what is counted or measured), and the text then
defines it at first use.

| Symbol | Meaning | Chapter |
|---|---|---|
| $X$, $X_i$ | A random variable; observation $i$ of a sample | 2 |
| $x$, $x_i$ | A possible or observed value of $X$ or $X_i$ | 2 |
| $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ | A sample of $n$ observations | 2 |
| $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ | The observed data | 2 |
| $n$ | Sample size (number of independent observations); also the number of trials of a Binomial | 2, 3 |
| $Y_i$, $y_i$ | Response of observation $i$ in a model with a predictor; its observed value | 6 |
| $x_i$ | Value of the predictor for observation $i$ | 6 |
| $Y_{ij}$, $y_{ij}$ | Response of observation $i$ in group $j$; its observed value | 7 |
| $\mathbf y_j$ | All the observations of group $j$ | 7 |
| $n_j$ | Number of observations in group $j$ | 7 |
| $\overline X$, $\overline x$ | Sample mean of the random sample; of the observed data | 3 |
| $s^2$, $s$ | Sample variance (divisor $n-1$, as `var()` in R); sample standard deviation | 3 |

The index $i$ counts observations and $j$ counts groups, also when a group has only one
observation ($Y_j$). Lists are written with low dots ($x_1,\ldots,x_n$) and sums with
centred dots ($X_1+\cdots+X_n$).

# Probability and distributions

| Symbol | Meaning | Chapter |
|---|---|---|
| $P(X=x)$ | Probability that $X$ takes the value $x$ | 2 |
| $P(X=x\mid\theta)$ | The same probability for a given value of the parameter $\theta$ (read the bar as "for a given value of") | 4 |
| $f_X(x)$ | Probability density of a continuous $X$ at $x$ (not a probability) | 2 |
| $F_X(x)$ | Cumulative probability $P(X\leq x)$ | 2 |
| $q_\alpha$ | Quantile: the value below which $X$ falls with probability $\alpha$ | 2 |
| $z_{0.975}$ | The 0.975 quantile of the standard Normal distribution (about 1.96) | 3 |
| $E[X]$ | Expected value (mean) of $X$ | 2 |
| $\operatorname{Var}(X)$, $\operatorname{SD}(X)$ | Variance and standard deviation of $X$ | 2 |
| $X\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda)$ | $X$ follows a Poisson distribution with mean $\lambda$ | 2 |
| $\overset{\mathrm{approx}}{\sim}$ | "Is approximately distributed as" | 3 |

Names of distributions are upright and capitalised inside equations, as in the text:
$\operatorname{Binomial}$, $\operatorname{Poisson}$, $\operatorname{NegBin}$ (Negative
Binomial), $\operatorname{Normal}$, $\operatorname{LogNormal}$, $\operatorname{Gamma}$,
$\operatorname{Beta}$ and $\operatorname{Beta-Binomial}$.

The parameters of the distributions of the course have these symbols. The [Supplement on
distributions](distributions.qmd) gives the formulas and the R functions.

| Distribution | Parameters | Mean and variance |
|---|---|---|
| Binomial | number of trials $n$, probability $p$ | $np$; $np(1-p)$ |
| Poisson | mean $\lambda$ | $\lambda$; $\lambda$ |
| Negative Binomial, $\operatorname{NegBin}(\mu,k)$ | mean $\mu$, shape $k$ | $\mu$; $\mu+\mu^2/k$ |
| Normal, $\operatorname{Normal}(\mu,\sigma^2)$ | mean $\mu$, variance $\sigma^2$ (R's `sd` is $\sigma$) | $\mu$; $\sigma^2$ |
| LogNormal | $\mu$ and $\sigma$ of $\log(X)$ | $e^{\mu+\sigma^2/2}$; median $e^{\mu}$ |
| Gamma, $\operatorname{Gamma}(k,r)$ | shape $k$, rate $r$ (or mean $\mu=k/r$ and shape $k$) | $k/r$; $k/r^2$ |
| Beta | shapes $a$ and $b$ (or mean $p$ and precision $\kappa=a+b$) | $a/(a+b)$ |
| Beta-Binomial | number of trials, mean probability $p$, precision $\kappa$ | |
| Zero-inflated distributions | probability of an extra zero $p_0$ | |

Note that the second argument of $\operatorname{Normal}(\mu,\sigma^2)$ is a variance. The
variance parameters of a model are written $\sigma^2$, with an upright subscript that
names the source of the variation when there are several ($\sigma^2_{\mathrm{obs}}$,
$\sigma^2_{\mathrm{group}}$).

# Estimation and likelihood

A **hat** marks an estimate or an estimator: $\hat\lambda$ is the estimate of $\lambda$.
Bold symbols are vectors or matrices and plain symbols are single numbers.

| Symbol | Meaning | Chapter |
|---|---|---|
| $\theta$ | A parameter in general | 3 |
| $\boldsymbol\theta$ | All the parameters of a model, as a vector | 6 |
| $\theta_0$ | The value of a parameter used to simulate data | 4 |
| $\hat\theta$ | Estimator or estimate of $\theta$ | 3 |
| $\operatorname{Bias}(\hat\theta)$, $\operatorname{MSE}(\hat\theta)$ | Bias and mean squared error of an estimator | 3 |
| $\operatorname{SE}(\hat\theta)$ | Standard error: the standard deviation of the estimator across hypothetical samples | 3 |
| $\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\hat\theta)$ | The standard error estimated from the data | 3 |
| $\hat\theta\pm z_{0.975}\,\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\hat\theta)$ | Wald confidence interval at 95% | 4 |
| $L(\theta\mid x_1,\ldots,x_n)$, $L(\theta)$ | Likelihood; $L(\theta)$ once the data are fixed | 4 |
| $\ell(\theta)$ | Log-likelihood, $\log(L(\theta))$ | 4 |
| $-\ell(\theta)$ | Negative log-likelihood (NLL in the text) | 4 |
| $\ell(\theta)-\ell(\hat\theta)$ | Relative log-likelihood, used to draw likelihoods | 4 |
| $\ell_{\mathrm{prof}}(\theta_1)$ | Likelihood profile of $\theta_1$ (the other parameters re-estimated) | 4 |
| $K$ | Number of estimated parameters | 4 |
| $\mathrm{AIC}$, $\mathrm{AICc}$, $\mathrm{BIC}$ | Information criteria: $\mathrm{AIC}=2K-2\,\ell(\hat\theta)$ | 4, 6 |
| $\mathbf g$ | Gradient of the NLL: its slope with respect to each parameter | 8 |
| $\mathbf H$ | Hessian of the NLL: its curvature with respect to each pair of parameters | 4, 8 |
| $\hat{\boldsymbol\Sigma}$ | Estimated covariance matrix of the estimates | 4 |

When two estimators of the same parameter are compared, an upright subscript names the
method, for example $\hat\lambda_{\mathrm{MM}}$ for the method of moments; otherwise the
hat stands alone.

# Deterministic functions

| Symbol | Meaning | Chapter |
|---|---|---|
| $y=f(x)$ | A function of the input $x$ | 5 |
| $f(x;a,b)$ | The same function, showing its parameters after the semicolon | 5 |
| $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$ | Generic parameters: positions in a formula, whose role the text explains for each function | 5 |
| $f'(x)$, $f''(x)$ | First and second derivative of $f$ | 5 |
| $\dfrac{df}{dx}$, $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial a}$ | Derivative with respect to $x$; partial derivative with respect to the parameter $a$ | 5 |
| $\lim_{x\to\infty}f(x)$ | Limit of $f$ as $x$ grows without bound | 5 |
| $x_{\max}$ | Value of $x$ at which a function peaks | 5 |
| $x_{1/2}$, $t_{1/2}$ | Half-maximum: value of $x$ (or of time $t$) at which a saturating function reaches half of its asymptote | 5 |
| $\mu(x)$ | A curve whose value is the mean of the response at $x$ | 7 |

Generic functions use $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$. Ecological symbols are used only for a named
parameterisation, where each one has a meaning: the attack rate $\alpha$ and the handling
time $H$ of the Holling type II functional response, or the carrying capacity $K$, the
growth rate $r$ and the initial size $n_0$ of the logistic function.

# Grouped models

| Symbol | Meaning | Chapter |
|---|---|---|
| $u_j$ | Random effect: the deviation of group $j$ | 7 |
| $\mathbf u$ | The random effects of all groups | 7 |
| $\hat u_j$ | Predicted effect of group $j$ | 7 |
| $\sigma^2_{\mathrm{group}}$ | Variance among groups (with a descriptive subscript, such as $\sigma^2_{\mathrm{plant}}$) | 7 |
| $\sigma^2_{\mathrm{obs}}$ | Variance of the observations within a group | 7 |
| $a_j=a\,e^{u_j}$ | Value of a parameter in group $j$ | 7 |
| $a_{\mathrm{typ}}$ | Value of a parameter in a typical group ($u_j=0$) | 7 |
| $Y_{ij}\mid u_j$ | The response for a given value of the group effect | 7 |
| $L_j(\boldsymbol\theta)$ | Marginal likelihood of group $j$ (the group effect integrated out) | 7 |
| $\beta_{\mathrm{name}}$ | Coefficient of a predictor, named by an upright subscript | 7 |
| $\beta_0$ | Baseline of a linear predictor, when no parameter of the model names it | 7 |
| $M_j$ | Indicator of a level of a factor (1 or 0), a capital with the index of its unit | 7 |

The book writes the effects of predictors one by one, with named coefficients, and does
not use matrix notation in the mathematics ($X$ is reserved for a random variable). In R
the model matrix of a parameter is `X_<par>` and its coefficients `beta_<par>`.

# Letters with more than one meaning

A few letters serve two concepts, each defined where it is used:

- $k$ is the shape of the Negative Binomial and the shape of the Gamma; $K$ (capital) is
  the number of parameters in the information criteria and the carrying capacity of the
  logistic function.
- $a$ and $b$ are generic positions in a deterministic function and the two shapes of the
  Beta distribution.
- $g(\theta)$ is a function of the parameters (in the delta method), while the bold
  $\mathbf g$ is the gradient.
- $\mu$ is the mean of a distribution, and $\mu(x)$ a mean that changes with a predictor.
- $H$ is the handling time of the Holling type II response, while the bold $\mathbf H$ is
  the Hessian.

# Writing rules

These rules apply to every equation in the book:

- **Logarithms** are natural logarithms and their argument is always in parentheses, as in
  R: $\log(3)$, $\log(\lambda)$, $\log(2)/b$. Another base is a subscript before the
  bracket: $\log_{10}(x)$.
- **Logit** and its inverse also take parentheses: $\operatorname{logit}(p)$ and
  $\operatorname{logit}^{-1}(z)$.
- **Exponentials** are written as powers of $e$, such as $e^{-bx}$; $\exp()$ is used only
  for a tall or nested exponent.
- **Products** of numbers take $\times$ ($0.4\times 0.7$), and products of symbols are
  written side by side ($a\,x\,e^{-bx}$).
- **Upright letters** mark names that are not variables: descriptive subscripts
  ($\sigma^2_{\mathrm{obs}}$), criteria ($\mathrm{AIC}$) and units.
- **Units** follow a number with a slash and no "per": 0.2/week, 2.5 prey/day, 90 kg/ha.
